judge.label: LLM rubric score, fresh-context judge, self-assessed — not human QA.
judge.independence_caveat: This judge is a different model family and a fresh context: it saw only the judge prompt, the rubric and the lesson. It did not direct the project and did not author anything in it. It is still a language model scoring a language model's output, so the label applies: not human QA.

notes.bilingual_quality: The lesson declares bilingual: true, but every Ar field (titleAr, mdAr, defAr, itemsAr, showAr, whyAr, situationAr, optionAr, consequenceAr, and both knowledge checks' stemAr/feedbackAr/options) contains the English text verbatim. There is no Arabic anywhere — not translated Arabic, not machine Arabic, none. Scored against its own declaration per the applicability note: an Arabic-channel learner receives English, which fails the claim more severely than the 1-anchor of literal word-for-word rendering.
notes.accessibility_ip: Compliant but minimal — the 3 anchor exactly. No licensed content, denylisted terms, or colour-carried meaning, but the two definition cards carry decorative icons (🗣️, 📌) with no alt text or aria-label, and there is no evidence of any accessibility consideration beyond absence of violations. No teaching use is made of the constraints.

verdict_notes: Pedagogically this is strong: plausible misconception-driven distractors with feedback that names the error, a worked example whose whys carry real judgement, and a scenario with genuine friction. But the bilingual declaration is false — every Arabic field is English text, which scores 1 against the declared bilingual: true claim and trips the floor regardless of the other scores. Accessibility is bare-minimum compliant with unlabelled decorative icons.
